To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) girls are more likely to display a secure attachment compared to boys; (2) children from no risk samples are more likely to present a secure attachment compared children from risk samples; (3) children from risk samples are more prone to display disorganized attachment compared to those from non-risk samples; (4) there is no interaction effect between risk and age; (5) there is no moderation effect between gender and age.

(i) girls present a more positive attachment narrative than boys; (ii) the effect of risk is not moderated by age or gender; (iii) the effect of gender is not moderated by risk or age; and (iv) the effect of age is not moderated by gender or risk.

(a) girls present more secure and less disorganized attachment narratives than boys, (b) children from risk families present more insecure and especially disorganized attachment narratives, and (c) there are no significant interactions between risk status, gender, and age

the quality of children's narratives in middle childhood is influenced by gender, but not moderated by risk status and age, and that the quality of attachment narratives of children with risk factors is influenced by their risk status, but neither moderated by gender nor age.

the attachment classification of a child depends on the combination of risk and gender, and that the effect of risk is not moderated by age or gender.
